title: Why Can't You Draw a Circle and a Line at the SAME Time? ⭕
description:
Try it: draw a circle with your left hand and a straight line with your right, both at once. The line bends into an oval. Your hands are copying each other's homework: each hand is run by the opposite half of your brain, and the two halves chat all the time over a thick bridge of nerve fibres (the corpus callosum), so the circle's plan leaks into the line's. The proof: in a 1996 study, two patients whose bridge had been cut by surgeons (to treat epilepsy) drew two different shapes at once more accurately than people with the bridge intact. Weirder: people who have lost an arm but can still move its phantom bend the line too, while they "circle" with a hand that isn't there. Did your line bend? Yes or no?
